Analytic maps and derivative growth

Written and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Repeated differentiation of a composite function produces many terms. Smoothness controls each fixed derivative, but preserving a derivative-growth class requires one estimate for the entire sequence of orders. We prove that composition with any real-analytic map preserves every class considered in the preceding lessons, even when the dimensions differ or the map has critical points. A count of coefficients in finite Taylor polynomials supplies the required uniform bound.

The prerequisites are Derivative growth and finite-order localization, Propositions 2–3, and the proved integral Taylor formula. The scalar foundation, Section 13.5, proves the full finite-dimensional chain rule and the higher derivative tensors used below; Sections 13.7–13.10 supply the power series, exponential and smooth flat function used in the examples. No infinite Taylor expansion of a general smooth function is assumed.

Exercise 4 — replacing analytic by smooth (foundation). Show that an arbitrary smooth inner map need not preserve the analytic endpoint of the theorem.

Solution. Take and take for , for . The exact smooth-cutoff proof in Section 13.10 of the scalar foundation proves that this function is smooth and every derivative at zero is zero. It is positive immediately to the right of zero, so its zero Taylor series cannot represent it there. Thus it is not real analytic at zero. The composite with the analytic identity function is itself. The analytic assumption on the inner map therefore cannot be replaced by smoothness in the stated theorem.
